sentences.text: Brontomerus was a camarasauromorph sauropod that lived approximately 110 million years ago during the early Cretaceous.
The genus was named in 2011 with the type species Brontomerus mcintoshi, a name honoring physicist and sauropod expert John Stanton McIntosh.

Known from two fragmentary specimens representing a juvenile and an adult, the adult weighed around six tonnes and measured approximately 14 meters in length, while the juvenile measured about 4.5 meters and weighed approximately 200 kilograms.
Fossils were recovered from the Ruby Ranch Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation in eastern Utah, specifically at the Hotel Mesa Quarry in easternmost Grand County.

Originally collected in 1994 and 1995 by researchers from the Sam Noble Museum, the fossils were later named and described by an international team including Michael P. Taylor, Mathew J. Wedel, and Richard L. Cifelli.
The research team could not recover more complete specimens due to prior pillaging of the fossil site.
Brontomerus was assigned a new species status based on an oddly-shaped hipbone allowing attachment for unusually massive leg muscles.
The anchoring of large femoral protraction muscles suggests Brontomerus used them to move its legs forward powerfully.
Dr. Michael Taylor hypothesizes that Brontomerus's strong thigh muscles were likely used for functions other than speed.
One hypothesis is that Brontomerus's large leg muscles were used to control its unusually long legs.
Researchers suggest Brontomerus may have used its powerful kicks for mating competition or defense against predators like Utahraptor and Deinonychus.
In 2013, Mannion et al. classified Brontomerus as a basal somphospondyl but could not resolve its precise affinities.
In 2012, D'Emic considered Brontomerus a nomen dubium due to its fragmentary nature but suggested it belonged to Titanosauriformes.
Brontomerus lived from the Aptian to the Albian stages, between 121.4 and 100.5 million years ago.
